timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: How do you figure out what an attacker might target?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Threat modeling, Peter. It's a structured process: identify your assets, map your architecture, identify threats, and design mitigations. Microsoft's STRIDE framework is a great starting point.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Six categories of threats: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege. For each component in your architecture, ask: can it be spoofed? Can data be tampered with? And so on.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Data flow diagrams are essential. Map every entry point, trust boundary, and data store. Then apply STRIDE to each element. You'll find vulnerabilities you never considered.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Less time-consuming than being breached. Threat modeling during design catches architectural flaws that penetration testing can't. It's cheaper to fix in design than in production.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Vulnerability management is the operational side. Scan regularly with Nessus or Qualys. Prioritize using CVSS scores plus context - a critical vuln on an internet-facing server matters more than one on an isolated workstation.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Patch management is vulnerability management's execution arm. Establish patch cycles: critical vulns within 48 hours, high within a week, medium within a month. Test patches before deployment. And use virtual patching with WAFs when you can't patch immediately.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Interview tip: walk through a threat modeling exercise for a web application. Use STRIDE, create a data flow diagram, and explain how you'd prioritize findings. GRC and security architect roles always ask this.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I'm drawing a data flow diagram of my app right now. This is eye-opening.
